[b]The Citharo Line and its Tendencies[/b]

When we speak of the "Citharo line", we speak of the cumulative directives and policies that form the ideological basis of the Socialist International, based in the city of Citharo, Sanguivallis. That is, the general line of the International, obeyed by all parties, in pursuit of the overarching dream of the communist society. The "general line" is a fundamental principle of orthodox socialist thought, and is used to ensure the strict compliance of doxa and praxis to the overarching vision that Citharo has set for a more hopeful future. Therefore, the Citharo line, the general line, is the forcing of the unity of the parties. Outside of it, there can be no factionalism.

Well, that was the idea anyways.

In reality, while there is indeed a "Citharo line" of basic policies upheld by the International, these policies are so simplistic and axiomatic as to be rendered pointless as an independent ideology. Once, it used to be a unifying force, with strict dogmas that ought to be pursued to ensure a proper revolution, but no longer. Since the Astaniran Civil War, deviations have sprung up from the Citharo line, deviations that were necessary to the national and historical contexts in which they were formed. 

In Astanir, the people's revolution was led with the backing of the bourgeoisie, the greatest evil of the class conflict, in order to destroy the fascist powers that devoured the nation from within. In Gythena, no communist party was formed, instead a supreme commune of communes, which installed its own parallel government without the guidance of a revolutionary vanguard and in pursuit of an ideal that seemingly avoided the two-stage model of socialist thought. Even here, in the Socialist heartland of Sanguivallis, the laws of the Church are seemingly kept equal to the laws of the soviets. 

And thus, the "Citharo line" has been diluted, further and further, to accomodate the necessity of deviations, until there was nothing left to affirm but hatred of the opportunists and affirmation that one day, these policies and practices will converge into a singular, superimposing, and truly global revolution. The so-called "Statement of Policies" are still there, but they seem silent, eager to accept anyone and anything willing to adopt the revolutionary symbolism of the left without any of its struggles and ill-tidings. And so, while the Citharo line exists as a unifying force, its unity is weak and senile, and has led to a variety of different "tendencies" that officially did not exist on paper, though to ignore their existence would be a fool's errand.

[spoiler=[b]Factional Tendencies of the Socialist International[/b]]

[b]Normative Tendency[/b]

Cui Fang, Cui Jin, Kang Hongxin, Horano Benir, and Rakon Gilon formed what is known as the "Normative Tendency" within the Citharo Line. Among a rich host of labels, the Normative tendency is also sometimes known as the Qianxun Tendency, the Daijunists, the New Socialists, or the Center Tendency. The basic formulation of their tendency was simple: The party was the supreme power, above the state and the people, which through its deep understanding of the class conflict is endowed with the power to determine every aspect of national life. The party secretaries were to be involved in all sectors of society, from arts and entertainment to law and the academe, and this power may never be surrendered.

Under the Normative Tendency, the revolution must come from the countryside, with the vanguard formed by the proletariat themselves, who must wage a people's protracted war to draw imperialist forces deeper into their own territory to be destroyed and later supplanted. Therefore, those in the Normative tendency believe that the united front strategy is of utmost importance to ensure the total defeat of the people's enemy, and that even those unware of the people's revolution may nevertheless be soldiers of it. Normatives are generally not sympathetic to the bourgeoisie, who while remaining useful in the two-stage model, are nevertheless profiteers who must be carefully constrained to prevent the workers' state from relapsing back into capitalism.

The Normative Tendency followed the two-stage model for the transition to socialism, beginning first with advanced capitalism under a bourgeois revolution to eradicate feudalism and establish industry, then socialism through the proletariat revolution. Therefore, the bourgeoisie may play a role in the transition to socialism under the first stage, though Normative theoreticians stress the necessity to first establish the power of the state before the bourgeoisie can be trusted to act in the interests of civil society. Without the party and without socialist praxis, the bourgeoisie are fundamentally incapable of acting for the good of the people, and will eventually destroy them for their own benefit.

[b]Democratic Tendency[/b]

Pio Graci, Argo Lo Pilato, Menelao Impastato, Immacolata Terrasi, Caio Graci, and Cirino Sferrazza are the architects of the "Democratic Tendency", also known as the Elseyran Tendency, the Moderates, Renaissance Socialists, Gracists, or the Right Tendency. These were the moderates of the Socialist International, and ever since the Gythenan Revolution they've been the most powerful of the various political tendencies within the Citharo Line. Like the Normatives, the Democratic Tendency accepted the importance of political parties but believed in the importance of the popular front, that the socialist state cannot be led solely by the communist party but instead by a union of all the left in defense against fascist imperialism.

The Democratic Tendency was, as was typical in the Elseyran communist tradition, a deeply scholarly tendency, which believed in the Classical formulation of socialism. That is, that the revolution inevitably originates in a minority position, driven by urban academics, who were tasked with mobilizing the proletariat. Crucially though, the Democratic Tendency did not universally condemn the bourgeoisie, whom they believed could be reasoned with to adopt the socialist position, and to therefore participate in the revolution against the true people's enemy, which was imperialism. The Democratic Tendency believed that the bourgeoisie, and through them entrepreneurship remained compatible with the two-stage model and should be entrusted to support the workers in the gradual transition to socialism.

Like Normatives, those of the Democratic Tendency accepted the two-stage model, though they went a step further, conceptualizing the first stage as a long, drawn out process to redevelop private markets into a form known as "advanced capitalism", in which all industry was neatly concentrated in a set number of firms, bound to laws that guaranteed the rights of the worker, and which were fully subservient to the state which could intervene at any moment in these firms during moments of distress (which were inevitable under the socialist dialectic). It is only when advanced capitalism is achieved that the markets may be seized by the workers without compromising the state's ability to meet the needs of the whole nation.

[b]Soviet Tendency[/b]

The last and most extreme of the mainline tendencies within the Citharo Line was the Soviet Tendency, or simply known as the New Order, represented solely by Gythenan revolutionary Irja Evesti. Also known as the Left Tendency or the Unitarists, the Soviet Tendency was ideologically the most distant from the Citharo Line's mainstream policies, explicitly rejecting the concept of the vanguard party and of the professional revolutionaries, instead believing that the fate of revolution rested solely with the proletariat. The party was, therefore, merely a gathering of the most class-conscious within a revolutionary society, and must exclude the bourgeoisie in all forms.

Similar to the Normatives, the Soviet Tendency believed that the revolution emanted from the countryside, but was not led by a vanguard, instead by a "foundation" consisting of all the proletariat self-organized into communes or "soviets" against a bourgeois government. Consequently, the Soviet Tendency is considered far more cautious in instigating revolution, believing that the proletariat must first be wholly radicalized before it may triumph. However, if and when the proletariat are prepared, then the revolution must be sweeping, all-consuming, destructive, which must destroy all the institutions that once represented the Old Order so that the soviets may proceed unmolested in the steady march into the New Order.

Economically, the Soviet Tendency rejects the two-stage model, asserting that relying upon a capitalist stage risks trapping the revolution within a state capitalist framework, which in turn places the nation in the hands of the party bureaucrats rather than workers. Instead, the Soviet Tendency favors immediate collectivization through the soviets. Despite its vague similarities with council communism, however, the Soviet Tendency rejects soviet democracy, instead believing that upon victory, the soviets of a revolution ought to unify so that a command economy may be implemented and a central planning authority created to guide material production across all soviets.

[/list][/spoiler]

[spoiler=[b]Constitutional Directive 26[/b]][b]Constitutional Directive 26[/b]

Socialist Thýven posed a significant dilemma to the Socialist International. In more ways than one, the Thrømm were clearly aligned with the interests of the Soviet Tendency and the New Order. It was unable (or unwilling) to form a vanguard party, reluctant to conduct a revolution without the full radicalization of the people, and believed in the formation of communes to coordinate parallel to the declining liberal democratic framework. However, as Irja Evesti herself would point out, there were some complexities to be noted as well. 

Unlike in Gythena, the Thrømm were socially conservative and explicitly tied to religion, perhaps even using its cultural base as the justification for socialism, rather than historical materialism. Additionally, the revolution seemed to be contingent upon the direction of Piter Drømm, a liberal revisionist principally representative of the bourgeoisie rather than the workers. Additionally, the reforms necessary for the state's entry into socialism were being done through a liberal democratic framework, when the New Order demanded that these institutions be left on the wayside so that a new system may be forced immediately. Additionally, the Thrømm seemed intent on adhering to a two-stage economic model, with certain sectors still in the hands of private markets merely unionized for the good of the workers.

The Thrømm were unwilling to accelerate the revolution through a vanguard, but they continued to engage in parliamentarism. Irja Evesti and Cui Fang, representing the further-left markers of the International's political spectrum, would thus label events in Thrømm a "bourgeois revolution" that was yet to fully transition into a true proletariat revolution. Evesti in particular would be highly critical, accusing the Thrømm of practicisng "left opportunism" and operating under a framework that was prepared to transition to anarcho-syndicalism rather than socialism. Together, these critics would file for several motions to military intervene in the crisis to install a more appropriate system of government at the quickest possible time.

However, the Committee on Eastern Elseyr, dominated by moderates of the Democratic Tendency, would reject such motions, with Argo Lo Pilato and Immocolata Terrasi believing that Thrømm parliamentarism constituted the minimum program of the transition to socialism, and was therefore compatible with the Citharo Line provided they use federalization as an ideological stepping stone, with Lo Pilato in particular stressing that the Thrømm had already affirmed the necessity of the vanguard party, even if they held differing views as to its importance. 

To help ease tensions within the International, Social Renaissance Party [i]Capo [/i]Pio Graci would author his own dissertation concerning the revolution in Thyven, entitled [i]Direttiva costituzionale 26[/i] ("Constitutional Directive [of] 26"), which among other things recommended that the Thrømm:

[list=1]

[*]Begin the process of supplanting all local government units with communes, and to unify these communes under an assembly that was to become the highest organ of state power.

[*]Subordinate all executive, judiciary, and military offices under this highest organ of supreme power in accordance with the principles of democratic centralism.

[*]Organize a communist party that was to encompass the whole population of Thyven, or else the formation of a united front of parties able and willing to follow the Citharo line.

[list=a]

[*]The party must maintain a political bureau and a central committee, constituted by the most class-conscious intellectuals in the Thyvenic Revolution, and vetted by the Socialist International.

[*]This communist party must operate with a state-sanctioned party school, which shall teach cadres the basic principles of Citharo Line Socialism, and which shall be mandatory for those seeking membership in the state's communes.

[*]Party cadres must be registered in a list and regularly mandated to retake registration every five years to ensure their obedience to party orthodoxy.

[/list]

[*]Nationalize the churches and radicalize the clergy, who may retain their ecclesiastical offices, but as dual workers not just to spirituality but to the revolutionary cause of the proletariat.

[*]Send delegates to Citharo in preparation for the Second Conference of Discussions.

[*]Finalize military alliances with the Qianxun Socialist Republic, Sanguinian Democratic Republic, and the People's Republic of Astanir.

[*]Establish an armed forces beholden not to the old liberal democratic state but to the communist party and the people's revolution.

[*]Adopt a system of five-year planning, to be aligned with the preexisting five-year plans of the Socialist International member states.

[*]Negotiate a status of forces agreement to permit the stationing of Sanguinian and Qianxun military forces on Thyvenic soil as an observation mission.

[list=a]

[*]That this status of forces agreement must be limited to no less than at least 500 personnel, to be stationed in any military facility near to Thyven's largest city, Vsyjjla.

[*]That these forces may be permitted to observe Thyvenic forces currently committed to the Tallislandic Civil War.

[/list]

[*]Permit tech-sharing agreements in the civilian and military sectors.

[*]Implement an economic agreement with the Socialist International, similar to the Terrasi Memoranda in the Kingdom of Montfleur.

[/list]
[/spoiler]

[b]December 10-20, 2026: The Federation[/b]

The general feeling across Thýven was one of disorder, even as federalization had succeeded, the first congress of the peoples had failed to layout a coherent model for the implementation of federalisation. 

It was as a result of this fault that within the federal states factionalism had begun to rise again as communist agitators, socialist propagandists, monarchist reformers, and various old guard groups had begun to clash in the bars and coffee houses of the federation.

In the meantime, Erjk Malben had begun to organise the Communist Party of North Thýven as a model party, bolstered by the recently released constitutional directive no. 26 by Argo lo Pilato in sanguivallis which provided a more precise definition for the communist transition. 

It had become evident to Malben that Drømm was too pragmatic at times, managing to court the monarchists, communists, and other parties too well, without succumbing to the revolutionary fervor. Drømm was also too careful, which while understandable, did not lead to the completion of the formation of what Malben called, Great Thýven. Indeed, following the adjournment of the first peoples congress, Drømm had returned to his peach farm in Jassel, leaving governance in the hands of the princes of the principates, who in recent days seemed more and more likely to be displaced by the rising federal movements in each of the principates. 

Thus, Malben began to pressure Drømm to step down as interim head of state and hold a national plebiscite for the establishment of a centralised Thrømmic party consisting of the various groups which he courted, but unified under the common banner of shifting Thýven into a socialist state. However, Drømm, fearing Malben had other intentions, would refuse to step aside, stating his appointment by the princes themselves.

Unfortunately, the prince's support for Drømm had been far less than when he had initially entered office, federalisation had led to their own positions becoming something on a whim, and with the threat of being replaced, the princes would also seem to side pragmatically with Malben. Thus after a private meeting with Malben, the princes would announce the morning of December 13th that the office of the interim head of government would be vacated and replaced by the First Council, which would act as a collective head of government shared among the five princes and Malben, being Chairman of the Council. 

In the meantime, Drømm, shocked by the sudden coup of his position, would seek to utilise his fame to travel the principates and oversee the newly formed sub-councils that had begun to arise within the federations, some dating back to the October dissolution of the government. As he travelled, he noted the general disunity of ideology, some leaned left, others seemed to lean right, the princes were still held in esteem in some, while in others votes had begun to remove the princes and replace them with their own Chairperson. 

In the meantime, the nationalisation of the Bank of Tharkønn had sent ripples across Thývens financial sector as suddenly independent branches found themselves under the government regulations, which were a patchwork of older imperial and royal legislation passed by the Gøsfodde, with Lenstahl holding it together by mere whims. 

Thus Drømm, who had now become an emissary of the First Council for the other federal councils would suggest to Malben on December 19th that he begin a thaw in relations with the socialist international, who had been in frequent contact with the new government. Malben, having taken it into his own mind to do so, would therefore announce in a public memo that he and Drømm would be travelling to Citharo to Discuss the future of Thýven. With Lenstahl to act as acting-chairman of the First Council until the return of Malben and Drømm.
